newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russian budget hits snag but IMF pays up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russian budget hits snag but IMF pays up.

text.p: Russia's tough 1997 draft budget, drawn up to keep economic reform on track, risks falling at the first hurdle after leading deputies on Wednesday recommended parliament throw out the spending plan.
The State Duma lower house of parliament's budget committee urged deputies to reject the draft at its first reading on Friday, committee chairman Mikhail Zadornov said.

"The committee, by an overwhelming majority, recommended the rejection of the budget," Zadornov told reporters. He said committee members were unhappy with the revenue projections and had doubts about the proposed levels of tax collection.
The draft envisages spending of 524.34 trillion roubles ($96.7 billion), revenues of 433.64 trillion.
The deficit works out at 3.3 percent of gross domestic product, compared with a planned 3.85 percent this year.
Ministers have acknowledged the targets are tough but have said the budget will deliver lower interest rates and inflation of about 10 percent a year, half this year's levels.

The deficit is a key target by which the International Monetary Fund measures Moscow's economic performance and decides on monthly payment of tranches of a $10 billion, three-year loan agreed earlier this year.
The IMF board on Wednesday released the latest tranche of about $350 million but economists have said the Fund is keeping an eye on the figures in the 1997 draft.
The Fund delayed payment of an earlier slice of the loan because of concern over low tax revenues.
Tax evasion is a perennial problem in Russia and, ironically, success in curbing inflation has made it harder for the government to operate with what revenue it does get.

Monthly inflation has fallen from 17.8 percent in January 1995 to 0.3 percent last month. The State Tax Service said this week that tax collection was running at 75 percent of target levels in the first nine months of 1996.
Russian leaders have pledged to seek a return to economic growth next year. However, President Boris Yeltsin has repeatedly said living standards must be improved.

Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, beaten by Yeltsin in July's presidential election runoff, said the draft budget would not provide growth, meet social needs or satisfy the cash-strapped armed forces' requirements.

"We have already warned parliament and the government that this is not a budget but a list of statistics which does not answer vital questions and does not stimulate economic growth," he told a news conference.
He said the communists, who hold 157 seats in the 450-seat Duma, had questioned Finance Minister Alexander Livshits on the budget on Tuesday.
Communist chairman of the Duma's economic policy committee Yuri Maslyukov, a former head of the Gosplan Soviet planning agency, said the party had not decided its stance on the budget.
"Nonethless we think that the budget must be reworked from the position of those promises which we have heard this year.
Russian financial markets shrugged off the budget troubles, with share prices rising strongly on record volumes and T-bill yields falling to record lows on high foreign investment.

Prices are rising on Monday's announcement of better than expected credit ratings for Russia and news that Yeltsin has moved from hospital, where he was preparing for heart surgery, to a sanatorium where he is working.
Deputies also threw out a bill on Wednesday to tax proceeds from trading government securities and shares, which could have hit Russia's fledgling markets.
